sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Every turn names the prior speaker, e.g. turn 5 answers turn 4's language fix. [s2] Each turn names and answers the previous speaker. [s3] Turns 4-8 each name and answer the prior mind, e.g. turn 6 rebuts turn 5's shame claim.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 3 and 6 restate Foucault's position rather than respond to softened startup. [s2] Turn 2 answers a position the Communicator never took. [s3] Turns 1-3 are parallel openings with no cross-reference.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 adds new tension: wanting understanding while also wanting partner change. [s2] Turn 6 moves from face-saving to collaborating on a shared front. [s3] Turn 4 adds meta-communication; turn 9 adds timing: pause until negotiation is possible.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 repeats turn 3's power framing with little new distinction. [s2] Turns 5 and 8 repeat the Stoic's same point. [s3] Turn 7's drop-the-word-you advice is generic, not a new distinction.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Language vs flooding vs power framing set out in turns 1-3. [s2] Technique vs uncontrollable partner, turns 4-7. [s3] Shame-driven defense vs. habit of poor communication, carried into section E.
sub.limitation: [s1] Misses Gottman's complaint-versus-criticism distinction, the most direct tension in the user's question. [s2] Turn 9's 'clash of egos' arrives with no time to explore it. [s3] Never asks whether raising hurt is criticism, the user's actual sticking point.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 absorbs the 'moral stick' point into needs-based framing. [s2] Turn 7 combines the Stoic's limit with clearer observation. [s3] Turn 8 drops the shame-only claim and takes up the Systems Thinker's view.
sub.limitation: [s1] Power Structuralist never shifts; turn 6 says only 'my previous point stands'. [s2] The Social Architect and the Communicator barely reshape each other. [s3] The Negotiator never revises in response to turns 4 and 5.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Section D sharpens validation of pain versus demand for admission of wrong. [s2] Turn 9 sharpens the question: does the partner want resolution or standing? [s3] Turn 9 names heard vs. avoid conflict as often incompatible in the moment.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 ends on partner's 'defensive wall', blurring rather than sharpening the question. [s2] Ends close to where section A started. [s3] The ending repeats the opening split between shame and pattern.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 fairly restates Rosenberg's wording focus before challenging it. [s2] Turn 6 accurately states the Stoic's detachment before answering. [s3] Turn 6 states turn 5's assumption accurately: a fixed state of shame.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7 drops a claim ('structure irrelevant') that the Empathic Communicator never made. [s2] Turn 2 attacks a straw man ('assumes partner is responsible for user's peace'). [s3] Turn 4 reduces the Negotiator to logic, which is a weaker version of interests.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: perfect language fails if the partner feels under siege. [s2] Turn 5: even perfect words may still be heard as criticism. [s3] Turn 5: a new method may itself get labelled as criticism.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3's 'disciplinary framework' objection is asserted, not argued against turn 2. [s2] Turn 3's 'misses the point' is asserted without a reason. [s3] Objections assert outcomes rather than giving evidence or causes.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Gottman's flooding and softened startup are accurately attributed in turns 2 and 5. [s2] Rosenberg's observation/evaluation distinction is faithful (turn 1). [s3] Real books; Getting to Yes ch. 2 fits separate people from problem.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 stretches Discipline and Punish's penal analysis onto a couple's conversation. [s2] Turn 2's quote doesn't match the cited Carter text; 'face' comes from Goffman's On Face-Work. [s3] Turn 7's never-say-you rule is closer to I-statement advice than Satir.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Frequent hedging: 'might be', 'perhaps the partner is already experiencing'. [s2] Consistent hedges ('might', 'perhaps', 'likely'). [s3] Hedged openings such as 'perhaps fears' and 'might be trapped'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 says 'the real issue is', stating a theory as fact. [s2] Turn 3 asserts the partner must defend face 'to survive the interaction'. [s3] Turn 7 'will surely retreat'; turn 6 'label loses its power' overclaim.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 offers a concession and keeps its core needs claim. [s2] Turn 7: 'I drop the claim that technique alone solves this.' [s3] Turn 8 explicitly concedes and drops the earlier shame-only claim.
sub.limitation: [s1] Concession targets an invented claim; turn 6 ignores turn 5's objection. [s2] The Stoic never concedes the user's legitimate need for repair. [s3] Turn 6's hard question about defensive partners is never answered.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A names the hurt-heard-as-attack stalemate accurately. [s2] Section A names the shame vs misunderstanding uncertainty. [s3] Section A frames it as a linguistic failure or a shame reaction.
sub.limitation: [s1] The 'how can we talk' request is mostly argued about, not answered. [s2] The Stoic reframes the question as the user's tranquility, not the couple's conversation. [s3] The user's own wording, 'how can we talk', gets little direct attention.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1 links the user's phrasing to the partner hearing judgment. [s2] Turn 1 ties directly to hurt heard as a judgment of character. [s3] Turn 2 uses the partner's 'criticizing' label specifically.
sub.limitation: [s1] Third-person 'the user' throughout; few details change the argument. [s2] Speaks of 'the user' in the third person; generic throughout. [s3] Third-person 'the user' throughout keeps the reasoning generic.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 ties needs focus to the user's goal of connection. [s2] Turn 6: 'the user likely wants connection, not just indifference.' [s3] Turn 9 ties to wanting to be heard without the fight.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6's autonomy framing displaces the user's stated aim of talking without fighting. [s2] Turn 8 subordinates the user's goal of talking to inner peace. [s3] Speakers' frameworks drive the debate more than the user's stated aim.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 notes timing: the partner may be 'under siege' already. [s2] Section E raises a possible structural lack of safety. [s3] Turn 5's walking-on-eggshells names a relational cost.
sub.limitation: [s1] Relationship stakes and the cost of the repeated argument are barely addressed. [s2] Never addresses the cost to the user of swallowing the hurt. [s3] Turn 7 invents that the user uses accusatory language.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E branches on whether defensiveness is physiological or moral. [s2] Section E branches on fragile self-image vs refusal to be vulnerable. [s3] Section E branches on shame vs. habit vs. unknown willingness.
sub.limitation: [s1] No focused question about what the hurts are or how they are raised. [s2] No questions put directly to the user. [s3] No focused questions, e.g. what exactly the user says or how often.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: wanting to be understood versus wanting the partner to change. [s2] Section D: seeking understanding vs forcing the partner to admit fault. [s3] Turn 9 separates the desire to be heard from the wish to avoid conflict.
sub.limitation: [s1] Raised once at turn 8 and never developed further. [s2] It appears only in the summary, not in the debate. [s3] Arrives only in the last turn and is not developed.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1 questions whether hurt is wrapped in evaluations of the partner. [s2] Turn 5 questions the assumption that better words fix the reaction. [s3] Turn 8: the user's reaction to being ignored may fuel the cycle.
sub.limitation: [s1] The user's assumption that their phrasing is neutral is not examined directly. [s2] Turn 2's assumption is assigned to the user without basis. [s3] Never tests the user's assumption that the partner's reply is deflection.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Section D: validation of pain versus partner admitting wrong. [s2] Turn 6: connection vs detachment. [s3] Turn 3 names safety and acknowledgement as shared needs.
sub.limitation: [s1] Conflicts between values are stated abstractly, without asking the user to rank them. [s2] Vulnerability vs self-protection is named in A but not developed. [s3] Does not ask which matters more to the user, repair or validation.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 recognises the partner's possible flooding without pathologising. [s2] Turn 3 frames the partner's defensiveness as protecting face. [s3] Turn 5 names eggshell fear; turn 2 names the partner's shame.
sub.limitation: [s1] The user's own fear, of not being heard, is never explored. [s2] The user's own fears are never explored. [s3] Turn 2's 'fragile self-image' edges toward pathologising the partner.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Section D offers 'A helpful reflection might be...' as an open question. [s2] Section D poses a question for the user to consider. [s3] Section E offers testable conditions the user can weigh.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 places the problem on the partner's wall, leaving the user little to own. [s2] Turn 8 risks implying the user should simply accept the defensiveness. [s3] Talking about 'the user' gives no direct questions to answer.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Section E sets out softened startup, collaborative reframing, and a test. [s2] Section D: careful speech vs acceptance. [s3] Options: meta-talk (turn 4), interests (turn 6), pausing (turn 9).
sub.limitation: [s1] Options never named in the debate itself; no option of waiting or third-party help. [s2] Options stay abstract; no concrete conversation format. [s3] The options are never set side by side as one choice.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: rephrasing alone is costless-seeming but fails without softened startup. [s2] Section E: accept the limitation vs address the lack of safety. [s3] Turn 9: being heard and avoiding conflict conflict in the moment.
sub.limitation: [s1] No cost given for reframing hurt as 'neutral goal' (section E). [s2] The costs of acceptance are never weighed. [s3] The costs of pausing or reframing are not stated.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E's if-physiological / if-moral-authority conditions are clear. [s2] Section E: fragile self-image vs refusal of vulnerability. [s3] Section E: shame-driven, so build safety first; habit, so use neutral language.
sub.limitation: [s1] Conditions are hard for the user to observe; no indicators given. [s2] No guidance on telling the two apart beyond one test. [s3] Gives no observable signs for telling shame from habit.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section E names partner willingness as the decisive unknown. [s2] Section A names one decisive uncertainty explicitly. [s3] Section D leaves trait vs. de-escalable reaction open.
sub.limitation: [s1] Major versus minor unknowns are not distinguished. [s2] Other unknowns, like history or frequency, go unranked. [s3] Does not separate major unknowns from minor ones.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Section E: test by asking help with a specific, neutral goal. [s2] Section E: test a small, neutral observation. [s3] Section E: pause, then invite a check-in at a neutral time.
sub.limitation: [s1] No concrete wording or timing; the debate turns give no steps. [s2] No example wording despite the NVC lens. [s3] No concrete wording or first sentence to try.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Turns 1 and 5 are plain and readable. [s2] Short, plain sentences. [s3] Plain terms: 'talking about how they talk'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3: 'disciplinary framework that mandates an admission of guilt' is abstract jargon. [s2] The third-person 'the user' distances the reader. [s3] 'Meta-communication' and 'interest-based negotiation' are left unexplained.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Speakers name whom they answer in every turn. [s2] Each turn names whom it answers. [s3] Each rebuttal names its target mind, e.g. turn 7.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7's dropped 'earlier claim' cannot be traced to any prior turn. [s2] Turn 6's 'shared front' is unclear in practice. [s3] Turn 8 'the user's own reaction' points to no earlier claim.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns, all within 25-65 words, evenly paced. [s2] Nine compact turns of 39-48 words. [s3] Nine turns of 40-50 words each, all within the rules.
sub.limitation: [s1] Uniform length and structure flatten rhythm. [s2] Turn 9 ends abruptly on a new question. [s3] Turn lengths are uniform, so the rhythm is flat.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Language, biology, power lenses are clearly separate. [s2] Three clearly separate lenses. [s3] Pattern, shame and interests stay distinct lenses.
sub.limitation: [s1] Voices sound alike in syntax despite different lenses. [s2] Only one explicit change of position (turn 7). [s3] The three minds share one clinical register.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Few recaps; each turn short. [s2] Little filler. [s3] Section D condenses the main insight usefully.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 3, 6, 9 repeat the same power claim. [s2] Turn 8 restates turn 5. [s3] Section E largely restates turns 5 and 6.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: experience invalidated 'regardless of how softly it is started'. [s2] The Stoic vs the Social Architect on detachment (turn 6). [s3] Turn 5: any new method may be relabelled as criticism.
sub.limitation: [s1] Stakes stay conceptual; no felt scene of the recurring argument. [s2] The stakes for the relationship are rarely felt. [s3] Stakes for the relationship are stated abstractly.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 concession is a small reversal. [s2] Turn 9 raises the partner's possible motive of protecting standing. [s3] Turn 8's concession shifts some weight onto the user.
sub.limitation: [s1] Reversal hinges on a claim never made, so it lands hollow. [s2] No real reversal. [s3] The reversal is mild and expected.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] Power Structuralist is distinctively stubborn. [s2] The Stoic's blunt 'That is a false hope.' [s3] The Negotiator's 'I suggest' gives slight individuality.
sub.limitation: [s1] Little personal voice; minds read like textbook summaries. [s2] The Communicator is bland. [s3] The minds read as interchangeable textbook summaries.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: hurt 'used as a moral stick'. [s2] Epictetus's control line (turn 2). [s3] Section D's 'defensive armor both partners wear'.
sub.limitation: [s1] No analogies or vivid examples elsewhere. [s2] No vivid examples or analogies. [s3] No vivid example, analogy or sharp line in any turn.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 opens a new turn of thought late. [s2] Turn 9 leaves an open, pointed question. [s3] Turn 9 settles into a calmer, conditional close.
sub.limitation: [s1] Flat, even intensity throughout all nine turns. [s2] Flat, even rhythm throughout. [s3] The intensity stays constant from turn 1 to 8.

strengths: [s1] Three genuinely distinct lenses (language, flooding, power) are clearly separated in turns 1-3.
[s1] Turn 8 surfaces a useful tension: wanting to be understood versus wanting change.
[s1] Section E gives clear conditional branches tied to the partner's type of defensiveness.
[s2] Rosenberg's observation/evaluation distinction (turn 1) is an apt, accurate entry point.
[s2] Section D's question, understanding vs forcing an admission of fault, invites real reflection.
[s2] Section E offers a low-cost test: a small neutral observation, then watch the response.
[s3] Strong continuity: turns 4-9 name and answer the prior mind directly.
[s3] Real revision: turn 8 concedes and drops its shame-only claim.
[s3] Section E gives clear conditional branches plus a testable pause-and-check-in step.
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 7 concedes a claim the Empathic Communicator never made, undermining honest revision.
[s1] Power Structuralist (turns 3, 6, 9) repeats a stretched Foucault reading without development.
[s1] Speaks of 'the user' in third person and offers almost no concrete way to talk.
[s2] Turn 2 (Stoic) straw-mans the Communicator; the quote doesn't match the cited Carter translation.
[s2] Turn 3 (Social Architect) draws 'face' from Goffman's On Face-Work, not the cited book.
[s2] Third-person 'the user' and no example wording leave the advice generic and distant.
[s3] Third-person 'the user' throughout keeps it impersonal, with no questions put to the user.
[s3] Turn 7 invents accusatory language; 'surely retreat' overclaims.
[s3] Flat textbook voices: no vivid example or concrete wording to try.
editorNotes: [s1] Require turns to address the user directly in second person.
[s1] Forbid conceding or rebutting any claim not actually stated in an earlier turn.
[s1] Require each lens to be applied to the user's question at the most direct concept (e.g. complaint vs criticism).
[s1] Require at least two turns to propose a concrete wording or step the user could try.
[s2] Require turns to address the user as 'you' and use the situation's specifics.
[s2] When quoting, the wording must match the linked translation exactly; otherwise paraphrase.
[s2] Require at least one concrete phrasing or script when a communication lens is cast.
[s2] Forbid rebuttals of positions the target never stated; quote or paraphrase the target first.
[s3] Require the minds to address the user as 'you' and pose at least one direct question.
[s3] Forbid assuming behaviour the user did not describe; turn such points into conditional questions.
[s3] Require one concrete script or example sentence the user could actually say.
[s3] Ask each mind for one memorable image or analogy grounded in its book.

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 builds directly on turn 6's meta-communication proposal. [s2] Turn 3 builds on Senge's loop; turn 8 tests the Analyst's experiment directly. [s3] Turn 5 disagrees explicitly with turn 4's abandoning of goals.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 rebuts 'detachment' at the Systems Observer, though the Stoic argued it. [s2] Turns 1-3 are mostly parallel openings that stake out lenses. [s3] Turns 3, 6 and 7 ignore the prior turn; mostly monologues.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 adds a meta-communication step beyond turn 3's loop diagnosis. [s2] Moves from intent vs structure (turns 4-5) to a primed protocol (turns 7-9). [s3] Turn 9 builds on turn 8's test: persistent defense means not about words.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7 repeats turn 4's intimacy appeal with modest new content. [s2] Turn 6's 'loss of nuance' adds little beyond restating the defensive mode. [s3] Turn 6's 'change' only sharpens turn 3 rather than developing it.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: framing versus loop rigidity, stated as the open question. [s2] Turns 4-5 test whether intent or structure drives the loop. [s3] Presence without resolution (turn 4) vs. a goal-directed joint project (turn 5).
sub.limitation: [s1] The possibility of legitimate criticism in the user's hurt is under-explored. [s2] Never examines whether the user's hurt is sometimes a legitimate critique. [s3] The validation vs. autonomy tension is asserted, not examined.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 Stoic revises toward examining demands; turn 8 uses Systems test. [s2] Turn 9: Systems Theorist combines I-statements with a structural boundary. [s3] Turn 9 uses the Negotiator's test as diagnostic evidence.
sub.limitation: [s1] Relational Ethicist never revises, dismisses turn 6 as 'clinical'. [s2] The convergence in turns 7-9 is somewhat tidy and quick. [s3] No mind qualifies its view in light of another's.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 leaves a sharper, testable fork than turn 1. [s2] Turn 10 sharpens it: soul of the relationship vs mechanics of the interaction. [s3] Section D sharpens it: reacting to content or to being addressed at all.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section D labels Systems Observer as 'fix the partner', misreading turn 6. [s2] Turn 10's claim that both are frightened appears late and is never examined. [s3] Turns 1-6 circle without clear accumulation.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 fairly takes the Systems Observer's proposal on its own terms. [s2] Turn 5 restates the Analyst's intent claim accurately before rebutting it. [s3] Turn 5 restates turn 4's position fairly before objecting.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 says the Stoic 'suggests you ignore the partner'; turn 2 never did. [s2] Turn 1 presumes the user brings a 'list of grievances', which is uncharitable to the user. [s3] Turn 2 agrees in name only, then switches the topic.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: meta-observation risks making partners 'observers of a machine'. [s2] Turn 4 challenges 'intent matters less' and gives the reason the system stays cold. [s3] Turn 5 explains why goals matter: a joint project instead of a battle.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4's challenge is aimed at the wrong speaker. [s2] Turn 5's locked-steering-wheel image argues by analogy, not evidence. [s3] Turn 6's power reading is never challenged by anyone.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Bateson's metacommunication (Play and Fantasy) and Epictetus Section 1 are apt. [s2] Senge's reinforcing loops and Kahneman's framing (ch. 34) are real concepts. [s3] Buber's I-Thou is applied fittingly in turn 4.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 invents 'When you say you want them to stop'; the user said no such thing. [s2] Kahneman stretched to threat detection; Buber cited for I-statements (turn 7). [s3] Getting to Yes credited to Ury alone; Care of the Self stretched to partner power struggles.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Most claims hedged with 'might' and 'perhaps'. [s2] Hedges like 'perhaps' and 'likely' in turns 1 and 3. [s3] Frequent hedges: 'might be', 'maybe', 'perhaps'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 and Section E infer the partner's refusal from one failed test. [s2] Turn 10 asserts 'you are both frightened' as fact; section D says 'We discovered'. [s3] Turn 2 'clearly confuses'; turn 9 'deep-seated resistance' overreaches.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: 'I concede that my previous point might have been too detached.' [s2] Turn 7: 'I will drop my initial claim that intent alone is sufficient.' [s3] Turn 6 announces 'I change my position'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3's strawman of the Stoic is never corrected. [s2] Turn 9's concession costs the Systems Theorist little. [s3] That announced change is not a real revision; no concessions appear.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A asks whether the problem is style or 'criticism' as a shield. [s2] Section A names the misreading-vs-delivery ambiguity. [s3] Section A asks whether the partner can hear vulnerability or the structure triggers combat.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 jumps to I-It diagnosis before clarifying the user's request. [s2] Turn 1 opens by recasting the user's hurt as criticism. [s3] The 'how can we talk' goal is only reached in turn 8.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 shapes a step around the repeated-argument pattern the user describes. [s2] Turn 8's script is built for the 'hurt heard as criticism' pattern. [s3] Turn 8 targets the specific 'criticism' trigger with a test.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7 assumes lost closeness 'you used to have', which the user never stated. [s2] Uses little beyond the one-line situation; much is generic. [s3] Turns 3 and 6 apply abstract theory with little tie to the details given.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 targets the user's goal: talk without the same argument. [s2] Turn 6 separates being heard from resolving the hurt. [s3] Turn 7 links the user's need for validation to listening.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 drifts toward Stoic peace, not the user's stated aim. [s2] Doesn't confirm the user's goal is mutual talk rather than acknowledgment. [s3] Turn 4 drops the user's stated goal of resolving the repeat argument.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 times the attempt 'during a calm moment'. [s2] Section E: a neutral third party if the partner can't regulate. [s3] Turn 8 sets a bounded 10-minute time frame.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 and 7 invent context: 'want them to stop', past closeness. [s2] Turn 7's 'forbidden' rule assumes the partner will cooperate. [s3] Turn 1 assumes the user treats the partner 'as an object' without evidence.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E branches on whether the partner is distressed by the cycle. [s2] Section E branches on whether the partner listens once safe. [s3] Section E: if still defensive, the issue is systemic, not linguistic.
sub.limitation: [s1] No focused question to the user about what was said or done. [s2] No focused questions about past episodes or the partner's view. [s3] Asks nothing about the context or history of the hurts raised.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 contrasts wanting closeness with wanting accuracy of complaints. [s2] Turn 6: want to feel heard vs resolve the underlying hurt. [s3] Turn 7 names a need for validation that may crowd out listening.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7's 'you are choosing to prioritize' edges toward declaring a hidden motive. [s2] The distinction is offered once and never developed. [s3] Turn 6 reads the desire for understanding as a demand for submission.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 asks whether pain is presented as a command to change. [s2] Turn 3: 'You might be assuming they understand your emotional vulnerability.' [s3] Turn 1 asks whether the user treats the partner as something to correct.
sub.limitation: [s1] Assumption that a single rephrasing is a fair test goes unexamined. [s2] Turn 1 imposes an assumption about the user rather than surfacing one. [s3] Framed as accusation more than an assumption the user can inspect.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Validation versus peace (turn 2) and closeness versus accuracy (turn 7). [s2] Turn 6: partner's safety vs user's connection. [s3] Turn 4 contrasts meeting each other with winning.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks the user which value matters most. [s2] The user's own priority ranking is never invited. [s3] The user's own priorities are never named or weighed.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Section A names the fear of triggering defensiveness; turn 6 notes mutual exhaustion. [s2] Turn 10: losing mutual trust hurts more than the disagreement. [s3] Turn 3 names the partner's fear of an imposed narrative.
sub.limitation: [s1] Fear is named in summary but not explored in turns. [s2] The fear is declared, not offered as a possibility. [s3] The user's hurt and fear are barely acknowledged; the power framing edges toward blame.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 leaves a fork the user can accept or reject. [s2] Section E's 'observe if their response changes' leaves the reading to the user. [s3] Second-person 'you might', plus turn 7's question to put to the partner.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section E's verdict ('their refusal') closes reflection prematurely. [s2] Section D's 'We discovered' presents conclusions rather than questions. [s3] Turn 9 closes on a verdict about the partner, not on the user's choice.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Options: rephrase, name the cycle together, or accept and detach. [s2] Options: framing experiment, third party, a single trial. [s3] Options: dwell in presence (turn 4), shared interests (turn 5), the test (turn 8).
sub.limitation: [s1] No option of couples help or postponing the topic. [s2] Doesn't frame what choice the user actually faces. [s3] Never framed as a choice among them, nor as waiting.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 weighs meta-observation against loss of intimacy. [s2] Turn 6 notes the partner's safety comes at the cost of the user's connection. [s3] Turn 5 implies the cost of giving up resolution.
sub.limitation: [s1] Cost of Stoic acceptance to the relationship is not weighed. [s2] The cost or risk of the 10-minute protocol is never discussed. [s3] Tradeoffs between presence and problem-solving are not spelled out.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: if partner is also distressed, meta-communication may work. [s2] Section E: willing when safe vs unable to regulate even when primed. [s3] Section E: a literal reading of words vs. the power of being called out.
sub.limitation: [s1] Condition for intentional deflection is hard to observe fairly. [s2] The conditions are about the partner only. [s3] Alternative reasons for the test failing, like timing or mood, are ignored.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 keeps framing versus loop explicitly undecided. [s2] Section E's 'If you are unsure' branch. [s3] Section D leaves content vs. the act of being addressed open.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section E treats one rephrased attempt as near-decisive evidence. [s2] Doesn't separate major unknowns from minor ones. [s3] Turn 9 treats one failed test as near-conclusive.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: ten minutes naming the cycle without discussing content. [s2] Turn 8 gives an exact opening sentence to try. [s3] Turn 8: a 10-minute hurt description without naming their actions.
sub.limitation: [s1] No guidance on what to do if the meta-talk itself escalates. [s2] Turn 7's 'forbidden from responding' rule is heavy-handed for a first step. [s3] Gives no next step for when the test fails.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Second-person, plain sentences, e.g. turn 6's 'Just name the cycle.' [s2] Turn 8's script is plain and usable. [s3] Turn 8 is plain and concrete.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1's 'it'/'thou' needs unpacking for most readers. [s2] I-It/I-Thou and System 1 are left unexplained for a lay reader. [s3] Turn 3 'internal sovereignty' and turn 6 'site of power' are opaque.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 clearly ties its claim to the Systems Observer's proposal. [s2] Turns name whom they answer ('The Analyst argues...'). [s3] Turn 5 names its target, 'The Interpreter about abandoning goals'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 names the wrong speaker for the 'detachment' objection. [s2] Turn 6's 'loss of nuance' has an unclear referent. [s3] Turn 6 'I change my position' does not say from what.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns, all within the word limit. [s2] Ten turns, all 48-65 words. [s3] Brisk turns of about 30 words; nine turns.
sub.limitation: [s1] Several turns near 60 words feel dense. [s2] Turns 1 and 6 crowd the word ceiling. [s3] Turns are too short to develop reasons.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Intimacy, control, and system lenses stay distinct throughout. [s2] Three lenses stay distinct; turns 7 and 9 mark the concessions. [s3] Presence, interests and power are clearly different lenses.
sub.limitation: [s1] Relational Ethicist and Stoic converge in turns 5 and 7 without marking it. [s2] The voices sound alike in syntax. [s3] The Historian's 'change' blurs whether its position moved.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Little recap; each turn adds something. [s2] Little repetition across turns. [s3] Little repetition; section E reuses turn 8 with purpose.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 4 and 7 overlap in their reach-for-closeness advice. [s2] Section D partly repeats turns 6-9. [s3] Section D restates turn 9 without adding to it.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9's fork: phrasing futile versus only lever you have. [s2] Intent vs structure conflict in turns 4-5. [s3] Turn 1: the partner hears 'a force trying to diminish them'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Tension softened by uniform hedging. [s2] The relationship's stakes stay abstract until turn 10. [s3] The tension is philosophical rather than lived.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: failure of the test 'could ironically lead to the peace you want'. [s2] Turn 10 reframes it: trust loss hurts more than the disagreement. [s3] Turn 6 recasts the desire for understanding as a demand for submission.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 reversal is quick and unexplained. [s2] The concessions in turns 7 and 9 are predictable. [s3] The surprise goes unchallenged and slightly implausible.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] Relational Ethicist's warmth versus Stoic's coolness are audible. [s2] The Analyst's insistence on 'soul' gives some character. [s3] The Interpreter's I-Thou voice is distinctive in turn 4.
sub.limitation: [s1] Systems Observer reads as procedural. [s2] The Behavioral Observer reads like a textbook. [s3] The Negotiator is flat and procedural.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: 'observers of a machine'; turn 1's 'it' versus 'thou'. [s2] Turn 8's ready-made sentence sticks. [s3] Turn 4: dwell in the moment of hurt with them.
sub.limitation: [s1] No vivid example of an actual exchange between partners. [s2] Turn 5's 'steering wheel already locked' analogy is muddled. [s3] No concrete scene or analogy anchors the ideas.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Moves from diagnosis to a step to an unresolved fork. [s2] The emotional turn at turn 10. [s3] The turn 8 test sets up turn 9's conditional verdict.
sub.limitation: [s1] Middle turns 4-7 share one emotional register. [s2] Turns 2-9 run at one even, clinical register. [s3] The emotional register barely shifts across turns.

strengths: [s1] Turn 6 gives a concrete, proportionate step: ten minutes naming the cycle together.
[s1] Turn 5's concession and turn 8's use of the Systems test show real integration.
[s1] Second-person address and apt grounding (Bateson's metacommunication, Epictetus Section 1) keep it relevant.
[s2] Real revision: turn 7 drops a claim and turn 9 integrates two views into a protocol.
[s2] Concrete next step: turn 8 gives a usable opening sentence that primes the partner.
[s2] Section E's branches turn the partner's response into a test the user can run.
[s3] A concrete, testable step: turn 8's 10-minute exercise, used diagnostically in section E.
[s3] Direct second-person address invites the user to reflect.
[s3] Distinctive lenses, especially turn 4's I-Thou presence over winning.
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 3 strawmans the Stoic and turn 4 rebuts the wrong speaker.
[s1] Turns 4 and 7 invent user context ('want them to stop', past closeness).
[s1] Turn 8 and Section E overclaim: one failed rephrasing proves the partner's refusal.
[s2] Turn 1 (Relational Analyst) accuses the user of objectifying the partner without evidence.
[s2] Accuracy stretch: Kahneman used for threat responses (turns 3, 6), Buber for I-statements (turn 7).
[s2] Turn 10 and section D state speculation ('you are both frightened', 'We discovered') as fact.
[s3] Weak responsiveness: turns 3, 6 and 7 ignore prior turns; no genuine concession.
[s3] Grounding slips: Getting to Yes credited to Ury alone; Foucault stretched in turns 3, 6 and 9.
[s3] Turns 1 and 6 blame the user (an 'object', 'demand for submission') without evidence.
editorNotes: [s1] Require each rebuttal to name the correct speaker and restate their claim accurately.
[s1] Forbid inventing user statements or history; turn missing details into conditional questions.
[s1] Require tests in Section E to state how much one result can and cannot show.
[s1] Ask one mind to explore the user's own fear or part in the loop without verdict.
[s2] Forbid an opening turn that presumes the user's fault; first state the user's reading charitably.
[s2] Require each mind's claim to match its book's actual argument, not a nearby popular idea.
[s2] Require naming the cost or risk of every proposed experiment.
[s2] Have one mind ask the user a focused question about a specific past episode.
[s3] Require each turn after turn 3 to answer a named prior claim, with at least one real concession.
[s3] Check that the full author list and the book's actual subject match the claim attributed.
[s3] Make turns long enough (40+ words) to give a reason, not only a reframe.
[s3] Forbid declaring motives for the user or partner; put them as questions.
